claim: FGFRs regulate multipolar neuron orientation and the morphological change into bipolar cells necessary to enter the cortical plate.
source: We have found that FGFRs regulate multipolar neuron orientation and the morphological change into bipolar cells necessary to enter the cortical plate.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract, supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: N-Cadherin cell-autonomously binds FGFRs.
source: N-Cadherin cell-autonomously binds FGFRs and inhibits FGFR K27- and K29-linked polyubiquitination and lysosomal degradation.
evidence: This claim is supported by co-immunoprecipitation experiments and cis/trans interaction assays shown in the manuscript.

claim: N-Cadherin inhibits FGFR K27- and K29-linked polyubiquitination.
source: N-Cadherin cell-autonomously binds FGFRs and inhibits FGFR K27- and K29-linked polyubiquitination and lysosomal degradation.
evidence: This is supported by ubiquitination assays using ubiquitin mutants shown in Figure 7.

claim: N-Cadherin inhibits FGFR lysosomal degradation.
source: N-Cadherin cell-autonomously binds FGFRs and inhibits FGFR K27- and K29-linked polyubiquitination and lysosomal degradation.
evidence: This is supported by experiments using lysosomal inhibitor leupeptin shown in Figure 7f.

claim: FGFRs accumulate and stimulate prolonged Erk1/2 phosphorylation when N-Cadherin inhibits their degradation.
source: Accordingly, FGFRs accumulate and stimulate prolonged Erk1/2 phosphorylation.
evidence: This is supported by Western blot data showing increased FGFR levels and Erk1/2 phosphorylation in Figure 8.

claim: Neurons inhibited for Erk1/2 are stalled in the multipolar zone.
source: Neurons inhibited for Erk1/2 are stalled in the multipolar zone.
evidence: This is demonstrated by in utero electroporation experiments with dominant-negative Erk1/2 shown in Figure 9a.

claim: Reelin prevents FGFR degradation through N-Cadherin.
source: Moreover, Reelin, a secreted protein regulating neuronal positioning, prevents FGFR degradation through N-Cadherin, causing Erk1/2 phosphorylation.
evidence: This is supported by experiments showing that Reelin treatment increases FGFR levels and Erk1/2 phosphorylation in a Rap1/NCad-dependent manner (Figure 8).

claim: Reelin causes Erk1/2 phosphorylation through N-Cadherin and FGFRs.
source: Moreover, Reelin, a secreted protein regulating neuronal positioning, prevents FGFR degradation through N-Cadherin, causing Erk1/2 phosphorylation.
evidence: This is demonstrated by Western blot experiments in Figure 8 showing Reelin-induced Erk1/2 phosphorylation that is blocked by FGFR inhibition or Rap1/NCad inhibition.

claim: Dominant negative mutants of FGFR1-3 induce accumulation of neurons at the MMZ.
source: shRNA against FGFR1, 2 or 3 and dominant-negative (DN) but not wildtype FGFR1, 2 or 3 induce an accumulation of neurons at the MMZ.
evidence: This is shown by in utero electroporation experiments and quantification in Figure 1a.

claim: shRNA against FGFR1 or FGFR2 induces an arrest of cells at the MMZ.
source: The knock-down of FGFR1 or FGFR2 using specific shRNAs also induced an arrest of cells at the MMZ, with a more pronounced phenotype when the two receptors are downregulated together (Figure 1b, Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is demonstrated by in utero electroporation with shRNAs and quantification shown in Figure 1b.

claim: FGFR1 and FGFR2 work redundantly with a prominent role in neuron migration.
source: These results suggest that FGFRs work redundantly with a prominent role for FGFR1 and FGFR2.
evidence: This is inferred from the combined knockdown experiments showing stronger phenotypes when both receptors are inhibited.

claim: FGFR1(DN) does not affect cell proliferation as measured by Ki67 expression.
source: FGFR1(DN) had no effect on the proportion of GFP+Ki67+ proliferative cells, GFP+Sox2+ apical neural stem cells or GFP+Tbr2+ basal progenitors (Figure 2a).
evidence: This is shown by immunostaining and quantification in Figure 2a.

claim: FGFR1(DN) does not affect apical neural stem cells as measured by Sox2 expression.
source: FGFR1(DN) had no effect on the proportion of GFP+Ki67+ proliferative cells, GFP+Sox2+ apical neural stem cells or GFP+Tbr2+ basal progenitors (Figure 2a).
evidence: This is shown by immunostaining and quantification in Figure 2a.

claim: FGFR1(DN) does not affect basal progenitors as measured by Tbr2 expression.
source: FGFR1(DN) had no effect on the proportion of GFP+Ki67+ proliferative cells, GFP+Sox2+ apical neural stem cells or GFP+Tbr2+ basal progenitors (Figure 2a).
evidence: This is shown by immunostaining and quantification in Figure 2a.

claim: FGFR-inhibited neurons are correctly specified as shown by normal Satb2 expression.
source: FGFR-inhibited neurons were correctly specified, as shown by the normal expression of Satb2, a marker for upper layer neurons born at the time of the electroporation.
evidence: This is demonstrated by immunostaining for Satb2 shown in Figure 2a.

claim: FGFR inhibition does not increase cell death as measured by activated caspase-3.
source: Immunostaining for activated caspase-3 showed no increase in cell death (Figure 2a).
evidence: This is shown by immunostaining for cleaved caspase-3 in Figure 2a.

claim: FGFR inhibition does not affect the number of neurites in multipolar cells.
source: Analysis of the morphology revealed no difference in the number of neurites or in the cell body length-to-width ratio of FGFR-inhibited multipolar neurons compared to control multipolar neurons (Figure 2b–d).
evidence: This is shown by morphological analysis and quantification in Figure 2c.

claim: FGFR inhibition does not affect the cell body length-to-width ratio of multipolar cells.
source: Analysis of the morphology revealed no difference in the number of neurites or in the cell body length-to-width ratio of FGFR-inhibited multipolar neurons compared to control multipolar neurons (Figure 2b–d).
evidence: This is shown by morphological analysis and quantification in Figure 2d.

claim: Fewer FGFR-inhibited multipolar neurons have their Golgi facing the cortical plate compared to control neurons.
source: However, while most control multipolar cells had their Golgi apparatus oriented towards the CP, fewer FGFR-inhibited neurons had their Golgi facing the CP, suggesting a failure to orient correctly (Figure 2e).
evidence: This is demonstrated by Golgi staining and quantification in Figure 2e.

claim: Most control neurons at the multipolar to radial transition zone have transformed into bipolar cells.
source: In addition, while most control electroporated neurons at the multipolar to radial transition zone had transformed into bipolar cells, FGFR-inhibited neurons were still mostly multipolar (Figure 2f).
evidence: This is shown by morphological reconstruction and quantification in Figure 2f.

claim: FGFR-inhibited neurons at the multipolar to radial transition zone are still mostly multipolar.
source: In addition, while most control electroporated neurons at the multipolar to radial transition zone had transformed into bipolar cells, FGFR-inhibited neurons were still mostly multipolar (Figure 2f).
evidence: This is shown by morphological reconstruction and quantification in Figure 2f.

claim: FGFR-inhibited bipolar neurons in the RMZ show no difference in leading process length compared to control cells.
source: Yet, the few FGFR-inhibited bipolar neurons migrating in the RMZ exhibited no difference in the length of the leading process and the cell body length-to-width ratio compared to control cells and possess an axon at the rear (Figure 2g–i).
evidence: This is shown by morphological analysis in Figure 2h.

claim: FGFR-inhibited bipolar neurons in the RMZ show no difference in cell body length-to-width ratio compared to control cells.
source: Yet, the few FGFR-inhibited bipolar neurons migrating in the RMZ exhibited no difference in the length of the leading process and the cell body length-to-width ratio compared to control cells and possess an axon at the rear (Figure 2g–i).
evidence: This is shown by morphological analysis in Figure 2i.

claim: Over-expression of wild-type FGFR1, 2 or 3 partially suppresses the migration defect induced by Rap1GAP.
source: Therefore, we tested for epistasis by over-expressing FGFRs when Rap1 is inhibited by the Rap1 GTPase-activating protein (Rap1GAP). The migration defect induced by Rap1GAP was partly suppressed by over-expression of wild-type FGFR1, 2 or 3 (Figure 3a).
evidence: This is demonstrated by in utero electroporation experiments and quantification in Figure 3a.

claim: Rap1 regulates FGFR1 protein abundance in vivo.
source: Therefore, we tested whether Rap1 regulates FGFR protein abundance in vivo. Since we could not reliably detect endogenous FGFR by immunofluorescence, we co-electroporated FGFR1-GFP and CherryFP with Rap1GAP or control plasmid in utero. The level of FGFR1-GFP in CherryFP+ neurons was reduced when Rap1 was inhibited (Figure 3b).
evidence: This is shown by in vivo imaging and quantification in Figure 3b.

claim: Over-expressing NCad-HA in cultured primary neurons increases the level of endogenous FGFR1.
source: In addition, over-expressing NCad-HA in cultured primary neurons increased the level of endogenous FGFR1 (Figure 3c), consistent with NCad mediating Rap1-dependent FGFR1 stabilization in vivo.
evidence: This is demonstrated by Western blot analysis in Figure 3c.

claim: NCad but not ECad increases protein levels of all three FGFRs in cultured cells.
source: As expected, expressing NCad but not ECad increased protein levels of all three FGFRs in cultured cells (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is shown by Western blot analysis in Figure 3—figure supplement 1a.

claim: FGFR inhibition does not change NCad protein abundance.
source: Control experiments showed that FGFR inhibition did not change the protein abundance of NCad and did not perturb NCad homophilic interaction properties (Figure 3—figure supplement 1b).
evidence: This is demonstrated by Western blot and co-immunoprecipitation experiments in Figure 3—figure supplement 1b.

claim: FGFR inhibition does not perturb NCad homophilic interaction.
source: Control experiments showed that FGFR inhibition did not change the protein abundance of NCad and did not perturb NCad homophilic interaction properties (Figure 3—figure supplement 1b).
evidence: This is demonstrated by co-immunoprecipitation experiments in Figure 3—figure supplement 1b.

claim: NCad can still accumulate at cell-cell junctions in the presence of FGFR1(DN).
source: NCad was still able to accumulate at cell-cell junctions in the presence of FGFR1(DN) (Figure 3—figure supplement 1c).
evidence: This is shown by immunostaining in Figure 3—figure supplement 1c.

claim: W161 of NCad is required for NCad-NCad binding between cells.
source: W161 of NCad (numbered from the initiator methionine, corresponding to W2 in the mature protein) is required for NCad-NCad binding between cells (Tamura et al., 1998; Pertz et al., 1999).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: NCadW161A does not bind NCad expressed on different cells.
source: As expected, NCadW161A did not bind NCad expressed on different cells (Figure 4—figure supplement 1a lane 2) but still bound NCad expressed on the same cell (Figure 4—figure supplement 1b lane 2).
evidence: This is demonstrated by trans interaction assays in Figure 4—figure supplement 1a.

claim: NCadW161A still binds NCad expressed on the same cell.
source: As expected, NCadW161A did not bind NCad expressed on different cells (Figure 4—figure supplement 1a lane 2) but still bound NCad expressed on the same cell (Figure 4—figure supplement 1b lane 2).
evidence: This is demonstrated by cis interaction assays in Figure 4—figure supplement 1b.

claim: NCadW161A rescues the movement of Rap1-inhibited neurons in vivo.
source: Remarkably, NCadW161A rescued the movement of Rap1-inhibited neurons in vivo (Figure 4), and increased FGFR1 protein level in vitro (Figure 4—figure supplement 1c).
evidence: This is demonstrated by in utero electroporation experiments and quantification in Figure 4.

claim: NCadW161A increases FGFR1 protein level in vitro.
source: Remarkably, NCadW161A rescued the movement of Rap1-inhibited neurons in vivo (Figure 4), and increased FGFR1 protein level in vitro (Figure 4—figure supplement 1c).
evidence: This is shown by Western blot analysis in Figure 4—figure supplement 1c.

claim: NCad EC4 is required for FGFR1 binding in vitro.
source: NCadΔEC4 no longer bound to FGFR1 in transfected cells (Figure 5a), although it retained homophilic binding to co-transfected NCad (Figure 5b).
evidence: This is demonstrated by co-immunoprecipitation experiments in Figure 5a.

claim: NCadΔEC4 retains homophilic binding to co-transfected NCad.
source: NCadΔEC4 no longer bound to FGFR1 in transfected cells (Figure 5a), although it retained homophilic binding to co-transfected NCad (Figure 5b).
evidence: This is demonstrated by co-immunoprecipitation experiments in Figure 5b.

claim: NCadΔEC4 fails to increase the protein abundance of co-transfected FGFR1.
source: Also, NCadΔEC4 failed to increase the protein abundance of co-transfected FGFR1 or to activate FGFRs, as observed by an increase in FGFR auto-phosphorylation on tyrosines 653/654 and phosphorylation of the well-known downstream signaling kinases Erk1/2 (Figure 5c).
evidence: This is shown by Western blot analysis in Figure 5c.

claim: NCadΔEC4 fails to activate FGFRs as measured by FGFR auto-phosphorylation on tyrosines 653/654.
source: Also, NCadΔEC4 failed to increase the protein abundance of co-transfected FGFR1 or to activate FGFRs, as observed by an increase in FGFR auto-phosphorylation on tyrosines 653/654 and phosphorylation of the well-known downstream signaling kinases Erk1/2 (Figure 5c).
evidence: This is shown by Western blot analysis in Figure 5c.

claim: NCadΔEC4 fails to induce phosphorylation of Erk1/2.
source: Also, NCadΔEC4 failed to increase the protein abundance of co-transfected FGFR1 or to activate FGFRs, as observed by an increase in FGFR auto-phosphorylation on tyrosines 653/654 and phosphorylation of the well-known downstream signaling kinases Erk1/2 (Figure 5c).
evidence: This is shown by Western blot analysis in Figure 5c.

claim: An FGFR inhibitor prevents NCad-induced FGFR auto-phosphorylation.
source: Finally, an FGFR inhibitor (Nakanishi et al., 2014) prevented NCad-induced FGFR auto-phosphorylation and phosphorylation of Erk1/2 (Figure 5c).
evidence: This is demonstrated by Western blot analysis with FGFR inhibitor treatment in Figure 5c.

claim: An FGFR inhibitor prevents NCad-induced phosphorylation of Erk1/2.
source: Finally, an FGFR inhibitor (Nakanishi et al., 2014) prevented NCad-induced FGFR auto-phosphorylation and phosphorylation of Erk1/2 (Figure 5c).
evidence: This is demonstrated by Western blot analysis with FGFR inhibitor treatment in Figure 5c.

claim: NCad binds FGFRs in cis, on the same cell, but not trans, between cells.
source: We also found that NCad binds FGFRs in cis, on the same cell, but not trans, between cells (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is demonstrated by cis and trans interaction assays in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: NCadΔEC4 does not rescue the migration of Rap1-inhibited neurons.
source: Importantly, NCadΔEC4 did not rescue the migration of Rap1-inhibited neurons (Figure 5d).
evidence: This is shown by in utero electroporation experiments and quantification in Figure 5d.

claim: NCad, NCadW161A and ECad all bind FGFRs in transfected cells.
source: In our hands, NCad, NCadW161A and ECad all bound FGFRs in transfected cells (Figure 6—figure supplement 1) but only NCad and NCadW161A increased the protein levels of co-transfected FGFRs (Figure 3—figure supplement 1a and Figure 4—figure supplement 1c).
evidence: This is demonstrated by co-immunoprecipitation experiments in Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: Only NCad and NCadW161A increase the protein levels of co-transfected FGFRs, not ECad.
source: In our hands, NCad, NCadW161A and ECad all bound FGFRs in transfected cells (Figure 6—figure supplement 1) but only NCad and NCadW161A increased the protein levels of co-transfected FGFRs (Figure 3—figure supplement 1a and Figure 4—figure supplement 1c).
evidence: This is demonstrated by Western blot analysis in Figure 3—figure supplement 1a and Figure 4—figure supplement 1c.

claim: NECad but not ENCad increases FGFR protein abundance.
source: NECad but not ENCad was able to increase FGFR protein abundance (Figure 6a).
evidence: This is shown by Western blot analysis in Figure 6a.

claim: NECad but not ENCad rescues the positional defect observed when Rap1 is inhibited in vivo.
source: Moreover, NECad but not ENCad rescued the positional defect observed when Rap1 is inhibited in vivo (Figure 6b).
evidence: This is demonstrated by in utero electroporation experiments and quantification in Figure 6b.

claim: NENCad but not ENNCad increases FGFR protein level.
source: NENCad but not ENNCad was able to increase FGFR protein level and rescue the positional defect observed when Rap1 is inhibited in vivo (Figure 6).
evidence: This is shown by Western blot analysis in Figure 6a.

claim: NENCad but not ENNCad rescues the positional defect observed when Rap1 is inhibited in vivo.
source: NENCad but not ENNCad was able to increase FGFR protein level and rescue the positional defect observed when Rap1 is inhibited in vivo (Figure 6).
evidence: This is demonstrated by in utero electroporation experiments and quantification in Figure 6b.

claim: NCad inhibits FGFR ubiquitination.
source: When FGFR1-Myc was co-expressed with HA-ubiquitin, a ladder of FGFR1-ubiquitin conjugates could be immunoprecipitated with antibodies against Myc (Figure 7a lane 3) or HA (data not shown). FGFR ubiquitination was inhibited by co-expressed NCad but not NCadΔEC4 (Figure 7a) or ECad (data not shown), consistent with NCad binding inhibiting FGFR ubiquitination.
evidence: This is demonstrated by co-immunoprecipitation and Western blot analysis in Figure 7a.

claim: NCadΔEC4 does not inhibit FGFR ubiquitination.
source: FGFR ubiquitination was inhibited by co-expressed NCad but not NCadΔEC4 (Figure 7a) or ECad (data not shown), consistent with NCad binding inhibiting FGFR ubiquitination.
evidence: This is demonstrated by co-immunoprecipitation and Western blot analysis in Figure 7a.

claim: ECad does not inhibit FGFR ubiquitination.
source: FGFR ubiquitination was inhibited by co-expressed NCad but not NCadΔEC4 (Figure 7a) or ECad (data not shown), consistent with NCad binding inhibiting FGFR ubiquitination.
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by data not shown.

claim: Co-expressing UbiK0 but not UbiWT increases FGFR1 protein level.
source: When co-expressed with FGFR1, HA-UbiK0 but not HA-UbiWT increased FGFR1 protein level and decreased FGFR1 ubiquitination (Figure 7b) suggesting polyubiquitination.
evidence: This is shown by Western blot analysis in Figure 7b.

claim: Co-expressing UbiK0 decreases FGFR1 ubiquitination.
source: When co-expressed with FGFR1, HA-UbiK0 but not HA-UbiWT increased FGFR1 protein level and decreased FGFR1 ubiquitination (Figure 7b) suggesting polyubiquitination.
evidence: This is shown by Western blot analysis in Figure 7b.

claim: Over-expressing UbiK27R or UbiK29R increases FGFR protein level to the same level as NCad.
source: We found that over-expressing UbiK27R or UbiK29R but not other mutants increased FGFR protein level to the same level as that induced by the presence of NCad-HA (Figure 7c).
evidence: This is shown by Western blot analysis and quantification in Figure 7c.

claim: Co-expression of UbiK27R or UbiK29R with NCad does not have any cumulative effect on FGFR levels.
source: Co-expression of UbiK27R or UbiK29R with NCad did not have any cumulative effect, suggesting that FGFR is degraded following attachment of K27- and K29-linked polyubiquitin and that NCad inhibits this process.
evidence: This is shown by Western blot analysis in Figure 7c.

claim: Both K27 and K29 ubiquitin linkages are required for FGFR degradation.
source: To test whether K27 or K29 linkages are sufficient or whether both are needed, we used ubiquitin mutants where all lysines except 27 or 29 are mutated to arginine (UbiK27 and UbiK29). Co-expressing together UbiK27 and UbiK29, which allows only K27 and K29 linkages, did not inhibit FGFR degradation (compare to UbiWT, Figure 7d). However, expressing either UbiK27 or UbiK29 inhibited FGFR degradation, suggesting that both K27 and K29 ubiquitin linkages are required for FGFR degradation.
evidence: This is demonstrated by Western blot analysis in Figure 7d.

claim: Overexpressing UbiK27R in utero partially rescues the multipolar migration of Rap1-inhibited neurons.
source: Importantly, preventing FGFR degradation in vivo by the overexpressing UbiK27R in utero partially rescued the multipolar migration of Rap1-inhibited neurons (Figure 7e).
evidence: This is demonstrated by in utero electroporation experiments and quantification in Figure 7e.

claim: Endogenous FGFR1 is degraded by the lysosome in primary cortical embryonic neurons.
source: Indeed, adding lysosome inhibitor leupeptin but not proteasome inhibitor epoxomycin to primary cortical embryonic neurons increased the protein abundance of endogenous FGFR1 (Figure 7f).
evidence: This is shown by Western blot analysis with inhibitor treatments in Figure 7f.

claim: Leupeptin but not epoxomycin increases levels of transfected FGFR1 to the same extent as over-expressed NCad.
source: Leupeptin but not epoxomycin also increased levels of transfected FGFR1 to the same extent as over-expressed NCad, suggesting that NCad protects FGFRs from lysosomal degradation (Figure 7—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is shown by Western blot analysis in Figure 7—figure supplement 1.

claim: Lysosome inhibition does not have a cumulative effect on FGFR1 in cells over-expressing NCad.
source: Lysosome inhibition did not have a cumulative effect on FGFR1 in cells over-expressing NCad, confirming that NCad protects FGFRs from degradation by the lysosome (Figure 7—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is shown by Western blot analysis in Figure 7—figure supplement 1.

claim: Treating neurons for 20 min with Reelin induces phosphorylation of Dab1.
source: As expected, treating for 20 min with Reelin induced phosphorylation of Dab1, a known rapid effect of Reelin (Howell et al., 1999), but did not activate Erk1/2 or increase FGFR1 levels (Figure 8a).
evidence: This is shown by Western blot analysis in Figure 8a.

claim: Treating neurons for 20 min with Reelin does not activate Erk1/2.
source: As expected, treating for 20 min with Reelin induced phosphorylation of Dab1, a known rapid effect of Reelin (Howell et al., 1999), but did not activate Erk1/2 or increase FGFR1 levels (Figure 8a).
evidence: This is shown by Western blot analysis in Figure 8a.

claim: Treating neurons for 20 min with Reelin does not increase FGFR1 levels.
source: As expected, treating for 20 min with Reelin induced phosphorylation of Dab1, a known rapid effect of Reelin (Howell et al., 1999), but did not activate Erk1/2 or increase FGFR1 levels (Figure 8a).
evidence: This is shown by Western blot analysis in Figure 8a.

claim: Reelin increases FGFR1 protein abundance after 15 hr treatment.
source: However, Reelin did increase FGFR1 protein abundance after 15 hr, consistent with inhibition of FGFR degradation and slow accumulation of FGFR1 over time (Figure 8b lane 4).
evidence: This is shown by Western blot analysis in Figure 8b.

claim: 15 hr Reelin treatment activates Erk1/2 to a similar extent as 20 min exposure to EGF or FGF2.
source: Remarkably, 15 hr Reelin treatment also activated Erk1/2, to a similar extent as 20 min exposure to EGF or FGF2 (Figure 8b lanes 2 and 3).
evidence: This is shown by Western blot analysis in Figure 8b.

claim: 15 hr treatment with R3-6 increases FGFR1 protein level.
source: FGFR1 protein level and Erk1/2 phosphorylation were also increased by 15 hr treatment with R3-6 (Figure 8c), a fragment of Reelin that is produced in vivo and is necessary and sufficient for Reelin regulation of neuron migration (Jossin et al., 2004; Jossin et al., 2007).
evidence: This is shown by Western blot analysis in Figure 8c.

claim: 15 hr treatment with R3-6 increases Erk1/2 phosphorylation.
source: FGFR1 protein level and Erk1/2 phosphorylation were also increased by 15 hr treatment with R3-6 (Figure 8c), a fragment of Reelin that is produced in vivo and is necessary and sufficient for Reelin regulation of neuron migration (Jossin et al., 2004; Jossin et al., 2007).
evidence: This is shown by Western blot analysis in Figure 8c.

claim: Reelin-induced Erk1/2 phosphorylation is completely abrogated by FGFR kinase inhibitor Debio1347.
source: Reelin-induced Erk1/2 phosphorylation but not FGFR1 accumulation was completely abrogated by FGFR kinase inhibitor Debio1347.
evidence: This is shown by Western blot analysis with FGFR inhibitor treatment in Figure 8b.

claim: Debio1347 does not inhibit Erk1/2 activation by EGF.
source: Debio1347 was specific because it inhibited Erk1/2 activation by 20 min FGF2 but did not inhibit Erk1/2 activation by EGF (Figure 8b) or Reelin-induced Dab1 phosphorylation (Figure 8—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is shown by Western blot analysis in Figure 8b.

claim: Debio1347 does not inhibit Reelin-induced Dab1 phosphorylation.
source: Debio1347 was specific because it inhibited Erk1/2 activation by 20 min FGF2 but did not inhibit Erk1/2 activation by EGF (Figure 8b) or Reelin-induced Dab1 phosphorylation (Figure 8—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is shown by Western blot analysis in Figure 8—figure supplement 1.

claim: Inhibiting Rap1 prevents Reelin-induced FGFR1 protein increase.
source: To test whether FGFR1 protein upregulation and Erk1/2 activation require Rap1 or NCad, cortical neurons were transfected with Rap1GAP or NCadDN, both of which inhibit NCad accumulation at the plasma membrane and inhibit multipolar migration (Jossin and Cooper, 2011). Inhibiting Rap1 or NCad prevented Reelin-induced FGFR1 protein increase and Erk1/2 activation (Figure 8d).
evidence: This is shown by Western blot analysis in Figure 8d.

claim: Inhibiting Rap1 prevents Reelin-induced Erk1/2 activation.
source: Inhibiting Rap1 or NCad prevented Reelin-induced FGFR1 protein increase and Erk1/2 activation (Figure 8d).
evidence: This is shown by Western blot analysis in Figure 8d.

claim: Inhibiting NCad prevents Reelin-induced FGFR1 protein increase.
source: Inhibiting Rap1 or NCad prevented Reelin-induced FGFR1 protein increase and Erk1/2 activation (Figure 8d).
evidence: This is shown by Western blot analysis in Figure 8d.

claim: Inhibiting NCad prevents Reelin-induced Erk1/2 activation.
source: Inhibiting Rap1 or NCad prevented Reelin-induced FGFR1 protein increase and Erk1/2 activation (Figure 8d).
evidence: This is shown by Western blot analysis in Figure 8d.

claim: Over-expression of Erk1DN induces partial migration arrest of multipolar neurons.
source: Over-expression of either Erk1DN or Erk2DN, but not wildtype Erk1 or Erk2, induced partial migration arrest of multipolar neurons (Figure 9a).
evidence: This is demonstrated by in utero electroporation experiments and quantification in Figure 9a.

claim: Over-expression of Erk2DN induces partial migration arrest of multipolar neurons.
source: Over-expression of either Erk1DN or Erk2DN, but not wildtype Erk1 or Erk2, induced partial migration arrest of multipolar neurons (Figure 9a).
evidence: This is demonstrated by in utero electroporation experiments and quantification in Figure 9a.

claim: Over-expression of wildtype Erk1 does not induce migration arrest of multipolar neurons.
source: Over-expression of either Erk1DN or Erk2DN, but not wildtype Erk1 or Erk2, induced partial migration arrest of multipolar neurons (Figure 9a).
evidence: This is demonstrated by in utero electroporation experiments and quantification in Figure 9a.

claim: Over-expression of wildtype Erk2 does not induce migration arrest of multipolar neurons.
source: Over-expression of either Erk1DN or Erk2DN, but not wildtype Erk1 or Erk2, induced partial migration arrest of multipolar neurons (Figure 9a).
evidence: This is demonstrated by in utero electroporation experiments and quantification in Figure 9a.

claim: FGFR1-3 are expressed in the VZ and MMZ of the developing cerebral cortex.
source: In the developing cerebral cortex FGFR1-3 are expressed in the VZ and MMZ (Iwata and Hevner, 2009; Hébert, 2011) (Allen Institute for Brain Science. Allen Developing Mouse Brain Atlas. Available from: http://developingmouse.brain-map.org/) and FGFRs have been associated with neurodevelopmental diseases including schizophrenia (O'Donovan et al., 2009; Terwisscha van Scheltinga et al., 2013), epilepsy (Coci et al., 2017; Okazaki et al., 2017), autism spectrum disorders (Wentz et al., 2014; Coci et al., 2017) and lissencephaly (Tan and Mankad, 2018), suggesting possible roles in neuron migration.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies and database references.

claim: FGFRs have been associated with schizophrenia.
source: In the developing cerebral cortex FGFR1-3 are expressed in the VZ and MMZ (Iwata and Hevner, 2009; Hébert, 2011) (Allen Institute for Brain Science. Allen Developing Mouse Brain Atlas. Available from: http://developingmouse.brain-map.org/) and FGFRs have been associated with neurodevelopmental diseases including schizophrenia (O'Donovan et al., 2009; Terwisscha van Scheltinga et al., 2013), epilepsy (Coci et al., 2017; Okazaki et al., 2017), autism spectrum disorders (Wentz et al., 2014; Coci et al., 2017) and lissencephaly (Tan and Mankad, 2018), suggesting possible roles in neuron migration.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

Available from: http://developingmouse.brain-map.org/) and FGFRs have been associated with neurodevelopmental diseases including schizophrenia (O'Donovan et al., 2009; Terwisscha van Scheltinga et al., 2013), epilepsy (Coci et al., 2017; Okazaki et al., 2017), autism spectrum disorders (Wentz et al., 2014; Coci et al., 2017) and lissencephaly (Tan and Mankad, 2018), suggesting possible roles in neuron migration.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

source: In the developing cerebral cortex FGFR1-3 are expressed in the VZ and MMZ (Iwata and Hevner, 2009; Hébert, 2011) (Allen Institute for Brain Science. Allen Developing Mouse Brain Atlas. Available from: http://developingmouse.brain-map.org/) and FGFRs have been associated with neurodevelopmental diseases including schizophrenia (O'Donovan et al., 2009; Terwisscha van Scheltinga et al., 2013), epilepsy (Coci et al., 2017; Okazaki et al., 2017), autism spectrum disorders (Wentz et al., 2014; Coci et al., 2017) and lissencephaly (Tan and Mankad, 2018), suggesting possible roles in neuron migration.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: FGFRs have been associated with lissencephaly.
source: In the developing cerebral cortex FGFR1-3 are expressed in the VZ and MMZ (Iwata and Hevner, 2009; Hébert, 2011) (Allen Institute for Brain Science. Allen Developing Mouse Brain Atlas. Available from: http://developingmouse.brain-map.org/) and FGFRs have been associated with neurodevelopmental diseases including schizophrenia (O'Donovan et al., 2009; Terwisscha van Scheltinga et al., 2013), epilepsy (Coci et al., 2017; Okazaki et al., 2017), autism spectrum disorders (Wentz et al., 2014; Coci et al., 2017) and lissencephaly (Tan and Mankad, 2018), suggesting possible roles in neuron migration.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Reelin is a secreted protein that regulates neuronal positioning.
source: Moreover, Reelin, a secreted protein regulating neuronal positioning, prevents FGFR degradation through N-Cadherin, causing Erk1/2 phosphorylation.
evidence: This is established knowledge in the field supported by citations throughout the manuscript.

claim: Projection neurons arise from the local VZ below the CP.
source: In general, projection neurons arise from the local VZ, below the CP, while interneurons migrate tangentially from the ganglionic eminences (Parnavelas, 2000; Rash and Grove, 2006).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Interneurons migrate tangentially from the ganglionic eminences.
source: In general, projection neurons arise from the local VZ, below the CP, while interneurons migrate tangentially from the ganglionic eminences (Parnavelas, 2000; Rash and Grove, 2006).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Projection neurons are layered in birth order with neurons born early in development below those born later.
source: The projection neurons are layered in birth order, such that neurons born early in development are below those born later (Takahashi et al., 1999).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: Major defects in projection neuron migration may underlie lissencephalies and heterotopias coupled with mental retardation.
source: Correct neuron layering is important: major defects in projection neuron migration may underlie lissencephalies and heterotopias coupled with mental retardation while milder defects are associated with mental disabilities including dyslexia, schizophrenia, epilepsy, and autism spectrum disorders (Bielas et al., 2004; Francis et al., 2006; Romero et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Milder defects in projection neuron migration are associated with dyslexia, schizophrenia, epilepsy, and autism spectrum disorders.
source: Correct neuron layering is important: major defects in projection neuron migration may underlie lissencephalies and heterotopias coupled with mental retardation while milder defects are associated with mental disabilities including dyslexia, schizophrenia, epilepsy, and autism spectrum disorders (Bielas et al., 2004; Francis et al., 2006; Romero et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Reelin activates Rap1A and RalA to upregulate surface levels of NCad.
source: One signal that regulates exit from the MMZ is Reelin, an extracellular matrix protein that activates the small GTPases Rap1A and RalA to upregulate surface levels of neural cadherin (NCad, CDH2) (Jossin, 2011; Jossin and Cooper, 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Inhibiting Reelin, Rap1 or NCad interferes with the orientation of multipolar neurons.
source: Inhibiting Reelin, Rap1 or NCad interferes with the orientation of multipolar neurons, increases sideways and downwards movements, and increases time spent in the MMZ.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Cell surface proteins including NCad, ECad, L1CAM and NCAM can bind to and activate FGFRs.
source: In addition to FGFs and heparan sulfate, cell surface proteins including neural cadherin (NCad or CDH2), epidermal cadherin (ECad or CDH1), L1 cell adhesion molecule (L1CAM) and neural CAM (NCAM) can also bind to and activate FGFRs (Williams et al., 1994; Williams et al., 2001; Suyama et al., 2002; Brown et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: NCad and FGFRs are highly expressed during the epithelial-mesenchymal transition of cancer cells.
source: Both NCad and FGFRs are highly expressed during the epithelial-mesenchymal transition of cancer cells and their interaction may be important for metastasis.
evidence: This is established knowledge in the cancer biology field.

claim: Tumor cells artificially over-expressing NCad require FGFR activity for metastasis.
source: Indeed, tumor cells artificially over-expressing NCad require FGFR activity for metastasis. Nevertheless, the role of NCad-dependent FGFR activation in metastasis pathology remains unclear (Hulit et al., 2007; Qian et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: FGFRs are needed for developmental steps that occur before migration, such as regional patterning of the cortex, neurogenesis and radial glia differentiation.
source: Second, FGFRs are needed for developmental steps that occur before migration, such as regional patterning of the cortex, neurogenesis and radial glia differentiation (Shin et al., 2004; Rash and Grove, 2006; Mason, 2007; Kang et al., 2009; Paek et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Cytoplasmic domain deletion mutants of FGFR1-3 are dominant negative because they form non-functional heterodimers with all FGFR family members.
source: Cytoplasmic domain deletion mutants of FGFR1-3 are dominant negative (DN) because they form non-functional heterodimers with all FGFR family members (Ueno et al., 1992).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: The NeuroD promoter is activated after cells leave the VZ.
source: To avoid effects on neurogenesis, DN mutants were expressed from the NeuroD promoter, which is activated after cells leave the VZ (Jossin and Cooper, 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: R3-6 is a fragment of Reelin that is produced in vivo and is necessary and sufficient for Reelin regulation of neuron migration.
source: FGFR1 protein level and Erk1/2 phosphorylation were also increased by 15 hr treatment with R3-6 (Figure 8c), a fragment of Reelin that is produced in vivo and is necessary and sufficient for Reelin regulation of neuron migration (Jossin et al., 2004; Jossin et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Erk1 and Erk2 double mutant mice exhibit a defect in cortical lamination.
source: Interestingly, Erk1 and Erk2 double mutant mice exhibit a defect in cortical lamination (Imamura et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: FGFR2 regulates neuronal migration and spine density.
source: While we were writing this manuscript, FGFR2 was reported to regulate neuronal migration and spine density (Szczurkowska et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a recent study.

claim: Defective FGFR2 mice show impaired core behaviors related to autism spectrum disorders.
source: While we were writing this manuscript, FGFR2 was reported to regulate neuronal migration and spine density (Szczurkowska et al., 2018). Defective mice showed impaired core behaviors related to autism spectrum disorders.
evidence: This is supported by citation to a recent study.

claim: The Reelin pathway regulates spine density and has been linked to autism.
source: Interestingly, the Reelin pathway also regulates spine density and has been linked to autism (Niu et al., 2008; Lammert and Howell, 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Reelin regulates the migration of dopaminergic neurons into the substantia nigra with induction of bipolar morphology.
source: Reelin was also reported to regulate the migration of dopaminergic neurons into the substantia nigra, with induction of bipolar morphology (Vaswani et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a recent study.

claim: NCad function in multipolar migration is independent of NCad-NCad trans interactions.
source: These results suggest that NCad function in multipolar migration is independent of NCad-NCad trans interactions but may require NCad binding to FGFR.
evidence: This is inferred from the rescue experiments with NCadW161A shown in Figure 4.

claim: Cell autonomous NCad-FGFR binding and activation are required to stimulate multipolar migration in vivo.
source: The requirement for EC4 to bind and activate FGFRs and to rescue migration supports the idea that cell autonomous NCad-FGFR binding and activation are required to stimulate multipolar migration in vivo.
evidence: This is inferred from the combined results of binding assays, activation assays, and rescue experiments.

claim: Cadherin EC4 interaction with FGFR is necessary but not sufficient to stabilize and activate FGFRs and regulate multipolar migration in vivo.
source: Overall, these data demonstrate that cadherin EC4 interaction with FGFR is necessary but not sufficient to stabilize and activate FGFRs and regulate multipolar migration in vivo. Additional unique features carried by NCad EC1-2 are also needed.
evidence: This is concluded from the chimera experiments shown in Figure 6.

claim: Additional unique features carried by NCad EC1-2 are needed to stabilize and activate FGFRs and regulate multipolar migration in vivo.
source: Overall, these data demonstrate that cadherin EC4 interaction with FGFR is necessary but not sufficient to stabilize and activate FGFRs and regulate multipolar migration in vivo. Additional unique features carried by NCad EC1-2 are also needed.
evidence: This is concluded from the chimera experiments shown in Figure 6.

claim: NCad may inhibit FGFR degradation as observed in some cancer cells.
source: The Rap1/NCad-dependent increase in FGFR protein in vivo (Figure 3b,c) and in vitro (Figure 3—figure supplement 1a) suggests that NCad may inhibit FGFR degradation, as observed in some cancer cells (Suyama et al., 2002).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a previous study and data in the manuscript.

claim: Degradation of many cell surface receptors involves ubiquitination of their cytoplasmic domains and targeting to the lysosome.
source: Degradation of many cell surface receptors involves ubiquitination of their cytoplasmic domains and targeting to the lysosome (Piper et al., 2014).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: FGFR is polyubiquitinated rather than multi-monoubiquitinated.
source: When co-expressed with FGFR1, HA-UbiK0 but not HA-UbiWT increased FGFR1 protein level and decreased FGFR1 ubiquitination (Figure 7b) suggesting polyubiquitination.
evidence: This is inferred from the experiment using UbiK0 mutant which prevents polyubiquitin chain formation.

claim: FGFR is degraded following attachment of K27- and K29-linked polyubiquitin.
source: Co-expression of UbiK27R or UbiK29R with NCad did not have any cumulative effect, suggesting that FGFR is degraded following attachment of K27- and K29-linked polyubiquitin and that NCad inhibits this process.
evidence: This is inferred from the lack of cumulative effect when combining NCad with ubiquitin mutants.

claim: NCad inhibits K27- and K29-linked polyubiquitination of FGFRs.
source: Co-expression of UbiK27R or UbiK29R with NCad did not have any cumulative effect, suggesting that FGFR is degraded following attachment of K27- and K29-linked polyubiquitin and that NCad inhibits this process.
evidence: This is inferred from the lack of cumulative effect when combining NCad with ubiquitin mutants.

claim: K27 and K29 polyubiquitin linkages target FGFR for lysosomal degradation.
source: The requirement for both K27 and K29 polyubiquitin linkages suggested that FGFR may be targeted for lysosomal degradation (Chastagner et al., 2006; Ikeda and Kerppola, 2008; Zotti et al., 2011).
evidence: This is inferred from the requirement for both K27 and K29 linkages and supported by citations to studies linking these linkages to lysosomal degradation.

claim: NCad protects FGFRs from lysosomal degradation.
source: Leupeptin but not epoxomycin also increased levels of transfected FGFR1 to the same extent as over-expressed NCad, suggesting that NCad protects FGFRs from lysosomal degradation (Figure 7—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is inferred from the similar effects of lysosome inhibition and NCad overexpression on FGFR levels.

claim: Reelin-induced Erk1/2 phosphorylation is dependent on FGFR activity.
source: Reelin-induced Erk1/2 phosphorylation but not FGFR1 accumulation was completely abrogated by FGFR kinase inhibitor Debio1347. Debio1347 was specific because it inhibited Erk1/2 activation by 20 min FGF2 but did not inhibit Erk1/2 activation by EGF (Figure 8b) or Reelin-induced Dab1 phosphorylation (Figure 8—figure supplement 1). These results suggest that Reelin-induced Erk1/2 phosphorylation is dependent on FGFR activity and correlates with its effect on FGFR protein levels.
evidence: This is inferred from the specific inhibition of Reelin-induced Erk1/2 phosphorylation by FGFR inhibitor.

claim: Reelin or R3-6 can activate FGFR1 signaling and Erk1/2 through the Rap1-NCad pathway.
source: Taken together, these results show that Reelin or R3-6 can activate FGFR1 signaling and Erk1/2 through the Rap1-NCad pathway.
evidence: This is concluded from the combined results showing Reelin/R3-6 effects on FGFR and Erk1/2 that are blocked by Rap1/NCad inhibition.

claim: Multipolar migration of projection neurons requires a Reelin-Rap1-NCad-FGFR-Erk1/2 pathway.
source: Overall our results suggest that multipolar migration of projection neurons requires a Reelin-Rap1-NCad-FGFR-Erk1/2 pathway.
evidence: This is the overall conclusion inferred from all the experimental results presented in the manuscript.

claim: FGFRs have overlapping functions during multipolar migration in vivo.
source: In this paper we report that FGFR1-3 have overlapping functions during the multipolar migration in vivo.
evidence: This is concluded from the redundancy experiments with multiple FGFRs.

claim: FGFRs are required downstream of Rap1 for multipolar cells to orient towards the CP, adopt bipolar morphology, and migrate out of the MMZ.
source: FGFRs are required downstream of Rap1 for multipolar cells to orient towards the CP, adopt bipolar morphology, and migrate out of the MMZ.
evidence: This is concluded from the epistasis experiments and morphological analyses.

claim: Rap1-dependent NCad upregulation stabilizes FGFRs by inhibiting K27- and K29-linked polyubiquitination and lysosomal degradation.
source: We found that Rap1-dependent NCad upregulation stabilizes FGFRs by inhibiting K27- and K29-linked polyubiquitination and lysosomal degradation and that NCad-FGFR cis interaction (on the same cell) is involved.
evidence: This is the main mechanistic finding supported by multiple experiments throughout the manuscript.

claim: NCad-FGFR cis interaction is involved in FGFR stabilization.
source: We found that Rap1-dependent NCad upregulation stabilizes FGFRs by inhibiting K27- and K29-linked polyubiquitination and lysosomal degradation and that NCad-FGFR cis interaction (on the same cell) is involved.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the cis/trans interaction experiments in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: FGFRs accumulate when NCad inhibits their degradation.
source: Consequently, FGFRs accumulate and are activated, resulting in prolonged activation of Erk1/2 when neurons are stimulated in vitro with Reelin.
evidence: This is inferred from the time-course experiments showing FGFR accumulation after Reelin treatment.

claim: Accumulated FGFRs are activated.
source: Consequently, FGFRs accumulate and are activated, resulting in prolonged activation of Erk1/2 when neurons are stimulated in vitro with Reelin.
evidence: This is inferred from the phosphorylation data showing FGFR and Erk1/2 activation.

claim: Inhibition of K27-linked polyubiquitination rescues the migration of neurons with inhibited Rap1.
source: In vivo inhibition of K27-linked polyubiquitination or overexpression of FGFRs rescues the migration of neurons with inhibited Rap1.
evidence: This is demonstrated by in utero electroporation with UbiK27R shown in Figure 7e.

claim: Overexpression of FGFRs rescues the migration of neurons with inhibited Rap1.
source: In vivo inhibition of K27-linked polyubiquitination or overexpression of FGFRs rescues the migration of neurons with inhibited Rap1.
evidence: This is demonstrated by in utero electroporation experiments shown in Figure 3a.

claim: This is the first physiological role for FGFR-NCad interaction during tissue development.
source: To our knowledge, this is the first physiological role for FGFR-NCad interaction during tissue development.
evidence: This is a claim about the novelty of the findings based on the authors' knowledge of the literature.

claim: FGFRs mediate Reelin activation of Erk1/2 to control migration during the multipolar phase.
source: Furthermore, we identified FGFRs as mediating Reelin activation of Erk1/2 to control migration during the multipolar phase.
evidence: This is concluded from the experiments showing Reelin-induced Erk1/2 activation is FGFR-dependent.

claim: FGFR-dependent Erk1/2 stimulation may be a key signal for orienting multipolar neurons towards the CP.
source: FGFR-dependent Erk1/2 stimulation may therefore be a key signal for orienting multipolar neurons towards the CP.
evidence: This is speculated based on the combined results showing FGFR and Erk1/2 are required for proper orientation.

claim: FGFRs have been implicated in migration of mesodermal and tracheal cells in Drosophila.
source: FGFRs have been implicated in other developmental cell movements, including migration of mesodermal and tracheal cells in Drosophila (Gisselbrecht et al., 1996; Lebreton and Casanova, 2016), neuroblasts in the mouse olfactory bulb (Zhou et al., 2015) and keratinocytes during repair of epidermal injury (Meyer et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: FGFRs have been implicated in migration of neuroblasts in the mouse olfactory bulb.
source: FGFRs have been implicated in other developmental cell movements, including migration of mesodermal and tracheal cells in Drosophila (Gisselbrecht et al., 1996; Lebreton and Casanova, 2016), neuroblasts in the mouse olfactory bulb (Zhou et al., 2015) and keratinocytes during repair of epidermal injury (Meyer et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: FGFRs have been implicated in migration of keratinocytes during repair of epidermal injury.
source: FGFRs have been implicated in other developmental cell movements, including migration of mesodermal and tracheal cells in Drosophila (Gisselbrecht et al., 1996; Lebreton and Casanova, 2016), neuroblasts in the mouse olfactory bulb (Zhou et al., 2015) and keratinocytes during repair of epidermal injury (Meyer et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: Directional information for FGFR signaling could be provided by an FGF gradient serving as a chemorepellent or attractant.
source: Conventionally, FGFRs are activated by FGFs and heparan sulfate proteoglycans (Ornitz and Itoh, 2015), so directional information could be provided by an FGF gradient, serving as a chemorepellent or attractant, as in the Drosophila trachea (Lebreton and Casanova, 2016).
evidence: This is speculation about possible mechanisms based on known FGFR biology.

claim: NCad may activate FGFRs in the absence of FGFs.
source: It is also possible that NCad activates FGFRs in the absence of FGFs. Reelin could stimulate FGFR-dependent Erk1/2 activity in cultured neurons in the absence of added FGF, suggesting that external FGF may not be needed in vivo.
evidence: This is speculation based on the observation that Reelin can activate FGFR signaling without added FGF.

claim: Co-clustering of FGFRs with NCad may be sufficient to activate the receptor independently of FGF.
source: The co-clustering of FGFRs with NCad may be sufficient to activate the receptor independently of FGF, with FGFRs acting as 'catalytic subunits' downstream of NCad.
evidence: This is speculation about the mechanism of FGFR activation by NCad.

claim: A similar mechanism of ligand-independent activation has been suggested for FGFR activation by the co-receptor Klotho.
source: A similar mechanism has been suggested for activation by the co-receptor Klotho (Lee et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: The E3 ligase responsible for FGFR ubiquitination remains unclear.
source: The E3 ligase and mechanism of lysosomal targeting remains unclear.
evidence: This acknowledges a gap in knowledge.

claim: The mechanism of lysosomal targeting of ubiquitinated FGFRs remains unclear.
source: The E3 ligase and mechanism of lysosomal targeting remains unclear.
evidence: This acknowledges a gap in knowledge.

claim: The function of NCad EC1-2 in regulating FGFR stability is unclear.
source: Their function is unclear. They may bind to a third partner in the complex that helps NCad inhibit FGFR degradation.
evidence: This acknowledges a gap in knowledge and offers speculation.

claim: NCad EC1-2 may bind to a third partner in the complex that helps NCad inhibit FGFR degradation.
source: Their function is unclear. They may bind to a third partner in the complex that helps NCad inhibit FGFR degradation.
evidence: This is speculation about the possible function of NCad EC1-2.

claim: A prolonged Erk1/2 activation might be required to induce a signal as is the case for EGF-induced neuronal differentiation of PC12 cells.
source: A prolonged Erk1/2 activation might be required to induce a signal as is the case for EGF-induced neuronal differentiation of PC12 cells (Traverse et al., 1994).
evidence: This is speculation supported by analogy to a known system cited from the literature.

claim: Erk1/2 signaling has been linked to transcription of matrix metalloproteinases genes.
source: For instance, Erk1/2 signaling has been linked to transcription of matrix metalloproteinases genes (Westermarck and Kahari, 1999) and some metalloproteinases are essential for the organization of the cerebral cortex (Jorissen et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Some metalloproteinases are essential for the organization of the cerebral cortex.
source: For instance, Erk1/2 signaling has been linked to transcription of matrix metalloproteinases genes (Westermarck and Kahari, 1999) and some metalloproteinases are essential for the organization of the cerebral cortex (Jorissen et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a previous study.
